title: Systematic review of the mutations in the active antigenic site Ø of the prefusion F protein of the Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) following the implementation of monoclonal antibody prophylaxis

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on mutations in the active antigenic site Ø of the prefusion F protein of Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) following the implementation of monoclonal antibody prophylaxis, specifically nirsevimab. The central question is whether these mutations affect susceptibility to nirsevimab.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A systematic search was conducted between January 1, 2022, and July 31, 2026, across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrial.gov for studies analyzing substitutions within the epitope of pre-F RSV protein, which is the target of nirsevimab, after the implementation of the mAb. The review included seven studies (five observational and two randomized controlled trials) with 2156 RSV-positive samples.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Most substitutions detected within the nirsevimab antigenic site reflect ongoing natural RSV evolution and do not significantly affect nirsevimab susceptibility. However, multiple RSV-B substitutions and combinations involving residues 64-68 and 204-208 demonstrated reduced susceptibility or high-level resistance.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review notes that resistance-associated variants were detected in 1.3% of RSV-positive samples and were exclusively among nirsevimab breakthrough infections. There is a gap in understanding the mechanisms behind these resistance variants and their potential impact on vaccine efficacy.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The detection of resistance-associated variants highlights the importance of continuous genomic and phenotypic surveillance to monitor the emergence and spread of resistant strains, particularly in RSV-B.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review examines mutations in the antigenic site Ø of the prefusion F protein of Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) following the use of monoclonal antibody prophylaxis, specifically nirsevimab. The review analyzed seven studies, including 2156 RSV-positive samples, and found that RSV-A strains showed limited variability with K65R being the most common substitution, while RSV-B strains demonstrated higher substitution frequencies, particularly involving I206M, Q209R, and S211N. Most substitutions were natural polymorphisms that did not affect nirsevimab susceptibility, but some RSV-B substitutions and combinations showed reduced susceptibility or resistance. Resistance-associated variants were detected in 1.3% of samples and were only found in breakthrough infections. The findings emphasize the need for ongoing genomic and phenotypic surveillance to monitor the evolution of RSV and its potential impact on nirsevimab effectiveness.

The review collates information on data accessibility and findability.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review identifies thirteen surveillance data sources for RSV, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2 in the U.S., with all but one being governmental. title: High respiratory syncytial virus burden in children under 3 years of age across all care levels in England.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This prospective surveillance study aimed to estimate the burden of laboratory-confirmed respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in under 3-year-olds in the United Kingdom.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was implemented in Merseyside and Bristol, encompassing 11 primary care sites, 5 walk-in centres, 2 secondary care hospitals and 2 tertiary care hospitals. Children aged under 3 years presenting with lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) symptoms were included, with a substudy in primary care recruiting children with upper respiratory tract infection (URTI).
analysis.methods: PRIMARY AND SECONDARY OUTCOME MEASURES: The primary outcome of the study was the prevalence of RSV infection in primary, secondary and tertiary healthcare settings. Secondary outcomes included severity outcomes (rates of hospitalisation and high dependency care admissions), risk factors for severe disease, economic burden of disease and coinfection prevalence.
analysis.main_results: 2000 children were included in the analysis (410 primary care and 1590 secondary/tertiary care). RSV prevalence was 50.0% (95% CI 46.7% to 53.3%) in children admitted to hospital via emergency departments (ED), 36.3% (95% CI 31.7% to 41.0%) in ED discharges, 36.5% (95% CI 24.7% to 49.6%) in primary care (LRTI) and 12.7% (95% CI 8.6% to 17.9%) in primary care URTI. Healthy term-born children accounted for 70.1% of RSV hospitalisations. RSV-positive cases incurred a higher mean cost per participant (£1811, 95% CI £1720 to £1903) than RSV-negative cases (£1295, 95% CI £1220 to £1370).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings revealed a substantial burden associated with RSV. Even moderate prematurity was a risk factor for severe disease, and these children may not benefit from maternal RSV vaccination due to missed late gestation antibody transfer.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results highlight the significant impact of RSV on young children and suggest the need for broader eligibility criteria for maternal RSV vaccination to include those with moderate prematurity.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was conducted in specific regions of England, which may limit generalisability. The evidence is strong as it is based on a large sample size and laboratory-confirmed cases.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to estimate the burden of laboratory-confirmed respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in under 3-year-olds in the United Kingdom. It was conducted across multiple healthcare settings in Merseyside and Bristol, including primary care, secondary care and tertiary care hospitals. The study found that RSV prevalence was highest in emergency department admissions (50.0%) and lower in primary care (36.5%) and URTI cases (12.7%). Healthy term-born children accounted for 70.1% of RSV hospitalisations, and RSV-positive cases had higher mean costs than RSV-negative cases. The authors concluded that RSV imposes a substantial burden on young children and that even moderate prematurity is a risk factor for severe disease. These findings suggest the need for broader eligibility for maternal RSV vaccination. The study's evidence is strong due to its large sample size and laboratory confirmation, but its regional focus may limit generalisability.

title: Maternal respiratory syncytial virus vaccination for infant protection: updated systematic review and meta-analysis of efficacy, effectiveness, and safety

analysis.scope_and_question: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a major cause of severe illness in infants and young children. The review aims to evaluate the efficacy, effectiveness, and safety of maternal RSVpreF vaccines for infant protection.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review updated the systematic analysis by searching MEDLINE, Cochrane Library/Central, Embase, and grey literature from 2000 to June 2025. It included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomised studies of interventions (NRSIs). Two independent authors performed screening, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment following standard methods. The PROSPERO registration number is CRD42023439128.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Meta-analyses of RCTs showed that maternal RSVpreF vaccines lowered medically attended RSV-related lower respiratory tract infections with vaccine efficacy of 68% (relative risk (RR) 0.32; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.13 to 0.77, 2 trials; 7,656 participants; high certainty of evidence (CoE)), severe RSV-related lower respiratory tract infections with a vaccine efficacy of 84% (RR 0.16; 95% CI 0.07 to 0.36, 2 trials; 7,656 participants, high CoE) and RSV-related hospitalisations with a vaccine efficacy of 70% (RR 0.30; 95% CI 0.15 to 0.61, 1 trial; 7,148 participants, high CoE) in infants. No safety signals were identified.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: There may be little to no difference in RSV-related mortality, all-cause mortality, vaccine-related serious adverse events, and intensive care admission. Requirements for invasive ventilation and duration of hospitalisation due to RSV disease were not reported by any trials. NRSIs suggested comparable effectiveness against hospitalisation, but certainty was very low (vaccine effectiveness of 72%; RR 0.28; 95% CI: 0.17 to 0.46, 3 NRSIs; 1,229 participants, very low CoE). Further research is required to clarify the long-term effectiveness of vaccines.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review highlights the need for additional studies to address the evidence gaps, particularly regarding the requirements for invasive ventilation and duration of hospitalisation due to RSV disease.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluates the efficacy, effectiveness, and safety of maternal RSVpreF vaccines for infant protection. The review includes RCTs and NRSIs, with a focus on RSV-related lower respiratory tract infections and hospitalisations. Meta-analyses of RCTs indicate significant reductions in medically attended and severe RSV-LRTI and RSV-related hospitalisations, with high certainty of evidence. However, there is limited evidence on RSV-related mortality, all-cause mortality, and serious adverse events. NRSIs showed comparable effectiveness against hospitalisation, but with very low certainty. The review concludes that maternal RSVpreF vaccination is effective in reducing RSV-related illnesses in infants, but further research is needed to address long-term effectiveness and other outcomes.

title: Exploring the Relationship Between Respiratory Syncytial Virus and Asthma Using Calendar Time at Birth as a Source of Quasi‐Random Variation

analysis.research_question_and_background: Observational studies suggest an association between severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and asthma, but it is unclear if this relationship is causal or confounded.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We investigated this relationship using calendar time at birth as a source of quasi‐random variation with respect to individual‐level risk factors for severe RSV infection. We analysed province‐wide linked administrative data for 1,437,731 infants born in Ontario, Canada, from 2002–2013.
analysis.methods: We used regression models to investigate the relationships between: (i) infant ages during the weeks with the highest incidences of RSV, influenza, and rotavirus hospitalisation and paediatric asthma; (ii) weekly incidences of RSV, influenza, and rotavirus hospitalisation and probability of paediatric asthma.
analysis.main_results: We observed the highest odds of asthma among infants aged 13–16 weeks during the RSV peak, 11–13 weeks during the influenza peak, and 16–19 weeks during the rotavirus peak. The relationship between weekly incidence of RSV hospitalisation and probability of paediatric asthma was small in magnitude; we estimated a 3.15 (95% confidence interval −0.07, 6.36) percentage‐point change in probability of paediatric asthma per 1 percentage‐point change in weekly incidence of RSV hospitalisation among infants.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: We found evidence supporting a limited causal role that did not fully explain the relationship between RSV and asthma. Other mechanisms, including seasonal factors, may contribute to previously reported associations.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that seasonal variation may play a role in the association between RSV and asthma, which could inform future studies on the mechanisms linking viral infections to asthma development.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its observational design and potential confounding factors, but the evidence is strong due to the use of large administrative datasets and regression models.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the potential causal relationship between severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection and asthma using calendar time at birth as a quasi-random variation source. The researchers analyzed province-wide administrative data for 1,437,731 infants in Ontario, Canada, from 2002 to 2013, examining the associations between RSV, influenza, and rotavirus hospitalizations and the development of asthma by age 5. They found that infants exposed to RSV during specific age windows had higher odds of asthma, but the relationship was small in magnitude. The study also noted an unexpected link between rotavirus seasonal variation and asthma. The authors concluded that while there is some evidence of a limited causal role, other mechanisms such as seasonal factors may explain the association. The study's findings highlight the need for further research into the complex interactions between viral infections and asthma development, with implications for understanding disease mechanisms and improving surveillance strategies.

title: Co-detection pathogen spectrum and risk factors for severe pneumonia in hospitalized children with respiratory syncytial virus: a targeted next-generation sequencing-based study

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) is the primary cause of lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI) in children. It is well-known that factors such as age, prematurity, and underlying comorbidities are associated with the severity of RSV, but whether the presence of co-detected pathogens is related to it remains unclear.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study included clinical data from children under 5 years of age who were hospitalized for LRTI and tested positive for RSV by targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) between August 2024 and December 2025 at Guizhou Hospital, Shanghai Children's Medical Center, Guizhou Province. The children were divided into severe groups (n=173) and non-severe groups (n=79) based on disease severity.
analysis.methods: Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were used to identify independent risk factors for severe pneumonia, and results were reported as odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI).
analysis.main_results: A total of 252 cases, 152 boys (60.3%) were admitted with RSV-positive LRTI. Severe disease was documented for 173 cases (68.7%). Patients with severe disease were younger than those with non-severe disease (median age, 7.8 months (IQR, 3.6~17.0 months) vs. 17 months (IQR, 8.8~26.5 months; P < 0.001). Staphylococcus aureus (OR = 3.25, 95% CI: 1.23~8.55, p = 0.017) and Pneumocystis jirovecii (OR = 2.59, 95% CI: 1.24~5.41, p = 0.011) were associated with severe disease, while RSV co-infected with other viral pathogens (OR = 0.30, 95% CI: 0.13~0.69, p = 0.005) and higher birth weight (OR = 0.52, 95% CI: 0.32~0.85, p = 0.008) showed a protective effect against severe RSV disease.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: This cohort study reveals the diversity of co-detected pathogens in children with RSV-positive pneumonia and identifies specific risk and protective factors associated with severe disease.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support prevention strategies for all younger children, including premature infants, with potential benefit for children aged 5 years or younger in specific high-risk groups.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on clinical data and the potential for confounding factors, but the evidence is strong due to the use of targeted next-generation sequencing and statistical analyses.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to describe the spectrum of co-detected pathogens in children with RSV-positive pneumonia and identify risk factors for severe disease. Using targeted next-generation sequencing, clinical data from 252 children under 5 years of age hospitalized for lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI) between August 2024 and December 2025 were analyzed. Children were divided into severe (n=173) and non-severe (n=79) groups based on disease severity. The study found that Staphylococcus aureus and Pneumocystis jirovecii were associated with severe RSV disease, while RSV co-infection with other viral pathogens and higher birth weight showed protective effects. These findings highlight the importance of considering co-detected pathogens and specific risk factors in the management of RSV-positive pneumonia in children, supporting targeted prevention strategies for younger children and those in high-risk groups. The study's evidence is moderate due to its observational design and potential for confounding factors.

analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Severe RSV disease imposes a substantial economic and health burden across the three tertiary hospitals studied in Argentina, Brazil, and Colombia.

analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Costs varied widely across sites but differed minimally by RSV status; differences between RSV-positive and RSV-negative episodes were small and non-significant in all three sites (all 95% confidence intervals [CIs] included zero).

These findings provide important evidence for informing RSV prevention policies in Latin America.

title: The Silent War of hMPV: Viral Interference with Host Immunity

analysis.scope_and_question: This review examines the primary mechanisms by which hMPV evades host immune responses.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: Although hMPV was identified in 2001, it remains less extensively studied than other major respiratory viruses, such as influenza virus and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), hindering the development of effective preventive and therapeutic strategies.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The virus disrupts early innate immune signaling pathways, particularly those involved in the induction and signaling of antiviral interferons (IFNs) and modulates inflammatory responses. At the level of adaptive immunity, hMPV impairs T-cell activation and the development of long-lasting immunological memory, which may contribute to susceptibility to reinfection. The virus also alters the functions of several immune and structural cell types, including macrophages, dendritic cells, and respiratory epithelial cells. In addition, hMPV may modulate host microRNA expression to promote immune evasion and prolong infection.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The recurrent nature of hMPV infections highlights the need to further investigate the immune-evasion mechanisms.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Such research is essential for developing safer and more effective vaccines, antiviral agents, and immunomodulatory therapies.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores how human metapneumovirus (hMPV) evades host immune responses, focusing on its impact on innate and adaptive immunity. The virus disrupts interferon signaling and modulates inflammatory responses, while also impairing T-cell activation and immunological memory. It alters immune cell functions and may modulate microRNA expression to prolong infection. These findings underscore the need for further research into hMPV's immune evasion mechanisms to improve vaccines and therapies. The review highlights the gaps in understanding hMPV's role in recurrent infections and its potential as a target for intervention strategies.

analysis.methods: Multinomial regression was used to impute likely causes of death when these were not laboratory confirmed. The variation in hospital admissions largely followed that of mortality.
analysis.main_results: In the second quarter of 2025 (2025/2), RSV mortality rate among children <5 years reached 60 per 100,000 - a 43% increase compared with 2024/2. title: Evaluating non-invasive respiratory samples for bacterial and viral pathogen detection by Nanopore metagenomics in community-acquired pneumonia
